clinicalPearls: A distinct primary liver carcinoma of adolescents and young adults, typically arising in a non-cirrhotic liver without underlying viral hepatitis or other chronic liver disease.
Characterised by the recurrent DNAJB1-PRKACA gene fusion, which is highly specific and increasingly used to confirm the diagnosis.
Presents with vague abdominal pain, a palpable mass, weight loss or malaise rather than the decompensation seen in conventional hepatocellular carcinoma.
Serum alpha-fetoprotein is usually normal or only mildly raised, distinguishing it from most conventional hepatocellular carcinomas.
Histology shows large polygonal eosinophilic tumour cells separated by parallel lamellae of dense collagenous fibrous stroma, giving the tumour its name.
Imaging typically reveals a large, well-circumscribed lobulated mass, frequently with a central scar and calcification that can mimic focal nodular hyperplasia.
Complete surgical resection, including of resectable nodal or limited metastatic disease, offers the best chance of prolonged survival as the tumour is relatively chemoresistant.
Lymph node involvement is common at presentation, so nodal assessment and aggressive surgical clearance are integral to management.
reference.pathophysiology: Fibrolamellar carcinoma is driven in the great majority of cases by a small deletion on chromosome 19 that generates the chimeric DNAJB1-PRKACA fusion gene. This fusion places the catalytic subunit of protein kinase A under the control of the DNAJB1 promoter, resulting in aberrantly increased and dysregulated protein kinase A activity that promotes tumour cell proliferation and survival. The neoplastic hepatocytes are large and mitochondria-rich, producing the characteristic deeply eosinophilic, oncocytic cytoplasm, and they are separated by abundant parallel bands of lamellar fibrosis produced by an activated stroma. Unlike conventional hepatocellular carcinoma, the tumour arises in an otherwise healthy liver without a background of cirrhosis or chronic hepatitis, and its biology, marker profile and demographic pattern are correspondingly distinct.
additionalInvestigations: multiphase contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen
MRI of the liver with hepatobiliary contrast
core biopsy with histopathology and immunohistochemistry (including CK7 and CD68)
molecular detection of the DNAJB1-PRKACA fusion
serum alpha-fetoprotein and other liver tumour markers
staging CT of the chest for pulmonary metastases
assessment of regional lymph nodes for surgical planning
redFlags: large or rapidly enlarging liver mass in a young patient
bulky regional lymphadenopathy or biliary obstruction
new pulmonary or peritoneal lesions suggesting metastasis
features of portal or hepatic venous invasion on imaging
constitutional symptoms with progressive weight loss
reference.prognosis: When completely resected, fibrolamellar carcinoma carries a more favourable outlook than conventional hepatocellular carcinoma, but frequent lymph-node involvement and a high recurrence rate temper long-term survival. Unresectable or metastatic disease responds poorly to systemic therapy and has a guarded prognosis.
pitfalls: Mistaking the central scar for focal nodular hyperplasia and delaying resection.
Excluding malignancy because alpha-fetoprotein is normal.
Assuming a cirrhosis-based hepatocellular carcinoma pathway in a young patient with a healthy liver.
Under-staging by neglecting regional lymph nodes, which are frequently involved.
Relying on systemic chemotherapy as primary treatment given the tumour's relative chemoresistance.

management: Pursue complete surgical resection with negative margins as the mainstay and only reliably curative treatment
Perform aggressive regional lymphadenectomy given the frequent nodal involvement
Resect isolated recurrences or metastases where feasible, reflecting the value of surgical clearance
Consider liver transplantation in selected non-cirrhotic patients with unresectable disease confined to the liver
Offer systemic therapy for unresectable or metastatic disease while acknowledging its limited efficacy, and encourage enrolment in clinical trials targeting the DNAJB1-PRKACA fusion
Undertake structured surveillance imaging after resection given the high recurrence rate
Manage within a specialist hepatobiliary multidisciplinary team
